newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zimbabwe maize alarms S.African, Zambian producers.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe maize alarms S.African, Zambian producers.

text.p: South African and Zambian maize producers are crying foul over possible cheap exports by neighbour Zimbabwe, which they say will threaten the livelihood of farmers in bordering areas.

The farming organisations said on Thursday there was evidence that Zimbabwe plans to dump excess maize at prices below those it can secure domestically, as it gears up to reap another surplus harvest this year.
The National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) in South Africa, the region's biggest producer, has asked the government to intervene to block any exports to the Northern Province.
"It looks like the Grain Marketing Board (GMB) in Zimbabwe has available to export in the vicinity of one million tonnes of maize," Nampo chairman Japie Grobler told Reuters.
"There is talk that there will be about 100,000 tonnes coming into the Northern Province. It is a net consumer area, so it will be detrimental to small farmers if there is dumping."
Grobler said Zimbabwe was looking at selling stock at around $120 a tonne, well below that country's average domestic price of around $150 a tonne.
The GMB could not be reached for comment on Thursday.
Zimbabwe is this year expecting another bumper crop of some 2.6 million tonnes. It has exported about 400,000 tonnes from its 1996 crop.

South Africa's crop, due to be harvested from May, is forecast at some 7.56 million tonnes. Although over two million tonnes below last year, it is still around a million tonnes in excess of domestic demand, topped up by hefty carryover stocks.

Grobler said a Zambian delegation, at a meeting on Thursday of representatives of maize-producing countries in the Southern African Development Community and producer bodies, had echoed Nampo's concerns.

"Zambia is extremely vulnerable to the dumping of maize by the Zimbabwe GMB and already prices of $125 a tonne are being quoted for delivery ex-GMB to Zambia and this is below the Zimbabwean domestic market price and therefore constitutes dumping," Grobler said quoting from a paper from the meeting.
Zambia, too, is expecting another surplus harvest of 15.3 million bags (90 kg each) this year, well above domestic consumption of around 12.5 million.
Andrew Fletcher, general manager of Zambia's Agricultural Commodities Exchange, told Reuters maize was currently selling at around $142 a tonne, some $100 down on last year.
"Our prices do not make it possible to bring in maize. It just would not be viable," he said.

South African maize traders played down Nampo's concerns. They confirmed that South Africa, as in previous years, would import some maize from Zimbabwe but that the amount would be tiny relative to South Africa's total crop.
"It will only be dumping if quantities are big and that will only happen if South African prices go up to unjustified levels, making Zimbabwe maize really attractive," a trader said.
"And in any case, I have had to pay more for maize in Zimbabwe than the Zimbabwe consumer," he added.
